questions.question: During the colonial period, the manufacturing sector accounted for only ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**10%.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• During the **colonial period**, the manufacturing sector contributed **only 0.1% to India's overall economy**. This reflects the limited development of industries and the colonial focus on exploiting raw materials rather than promoting industrialization.
 
• The manufacturing sector was neglected as the British government emphasized agriculture and the extraction of raw materials like cotton, jute, and minerals to export them to Britain for processing. *Hence, statement is correct.*
 
• Industrialization during the colonial period was restricted to a few sectors, such as textiles and jute, but these were primarily focused on meeting British needs rather than strengthening India's economy. *Hence, statement is correct.*
 
• The limited contribution of the manufacturing sector (0.1%) highlights the exploitation of India's resources and labor by the British and their failure to establish a robust industrial base in India. *Hence, statement is correct.*
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is 0.1.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Colonial Economic Policies:**

 
 
• The British implemented policies that focused on **exploitation of India's resources**. Raw materials were exported to Britain, and finished goods were imported back into India.
 
• India was reduced to a supplier of raw materials and a market for British goods, hindering the growth of domestic industries.
 
 
 
• **Impact on Manufacturing Sector:**
 
 
• The manufacturing sector in India was limited to basic industries like **textiles, jute, and iron**. However, these industries were not developed to their full potential.
 
• Most of the industrial production focused on **exporting goods** to Britain, leaving India's economy stagnant and dependent on agriculture.
 
 
 
• **Industrial Growth Post-Independence:**
 
 
• Post-independence, India focused on industrialization to recover from the stagnation caused by colonial policies.
 
• The **Five-Year Plans** introduced after independence emphasized the development of industries like steel, machinery, and textiles.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Colonial Legacy:**

 
 
• The British economic policies led to the **deindustrialization of India**. Traditional industries like handloom and handicrafts suffered due to competition with British manufactured goods.
 
• The lack of investment in infrastructure, technology, and skill development further hampered the growth of the manufacturing sector.
 
 
 
• **Post-Colonial Efforts:**
 
 
• Post-independence, India took measures to boost industrialization, including establishing public sector enterprises and encouraging private sector participation.
 
• Schemes like the **Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956** laid the foundation for economic growth.

questions.question: Which schedule of the Citizenship Act, 1955, contains the qualifications for naturalisation?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Third Schedule**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Third Schedule** of the **Citizenship Act, 1955** outlines the **qualifications for naturalisation**. Naturalisation is one of the ways to acquire Indian citizenship.
 
• To be eligible for naturalisation, an individual must meet specific criteria, such as a minimum period of residence in India, proficiency in an Indian language, and good character.
 
• An applicant must have resided in India for a total of **12 years** (11 years continuously and at least 1 year immediately before applying). Hence, the qualifications for naturalisation are specifically listed under the **Third Schedule**.
 
• The **First Schedule** of the Citizenship Act, 1955, deals with **countries to which citizenship by descent applies**. Hence, this is not related to naturalisation.
 
• The **Second Schedule** addresses **oaths of allegiance**, a requirement during the process of acquiring citizenship but not the qualifications for naturalisation. Therefore, this is also incorrect.
 
• The **Tenth Schedule** of the Indian Constitution is unrelated to the Citizenship Act, 1955. It deals with the **anti-defection law** concerning political parties. Hence, this is irrelevant to the qualifications for naturalisation.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Third Schedule.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Citizenship Act, 1955:**

 
 
• The **Citizenship Act, 1955**, provides the framework for acquiring, determining, and terminating Indian citizenship. It is divided into multiple sections and schedules for clarity.
 
• It prescribes five ways of acquiring citizenship: **by birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, and incorporation of territory**. Naturalisation is elaborated under the **Third Schedule**.
 
 
 
• **Naturalisation Process:**
 
 
• Naturalisation allows a foreign national to become an Indian citizen after fulfilling specific criteria set in the **Third Schedule**.
 
• The applicant must renounce any other citizenship held and swear allegiance to the **Indian Constitution**.
 
• **Example:** Individuals who have contributed to India’s development or have special achievements in science, art, literature, or humanitarian work may also be granted citizenship through naturalisation.
 
 
 
• **Features of the Third Schedule:**
 
 
• It outlines the **residence requirement** (12 years), **knowledge of Indian languages**, and other aspects like maintaining good character.
 
• It provides the criteria for the government to assess whether an individual is eligible for citizenship by naturalisation.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Legal Considerations:**

 
 
• Individuals applying for naturalisation under the **Third Schedule** must not only fulfill the residence requirement but also demonstrate their commitment to Indian society and its values.
 
• The process includes submitting an application to the **Ministry of Home Affairs** and undergoing verification procedures.
 
 
 
• **Notable Instances:**
 
 
• In some cases, the government may waive certain criteria under the **Third Schedule** for individuals who have significantly contributed to India’s development.
 
• The Citizenship Act was amended multiple times, including in **2019**, to add provisions for granting citizenship to specific persecuted communities from neighboring countries.

questions.question: According to the principle of collective responsibility in India’s parliamentary system, a successful no-confidence motion against a single Union Minister requires which action?

options.text: The Lok Sabha is immediately dissolved.
The entire Council of Ministers must resign.
Only the targeted minister must resign.
The President dismisses only the targeted minister.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The entire Council of Ministers must resign.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Principle of Collective Responsibility:** According to **Article 75(3)** of the **Constitution of India**, the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the **Lok Sabha**. This means that if a no-confidence motion is passed against even a single Union Minister, it is considered as a loss of confidence in the entire Council of Ministers.
 
• In such cases, the entire Council of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, must resign as they function as a collective entity. This ensures accountability to the elected representatives of the people and upholds the democratic framework of the parliamentary system.
 
• The Council of Ministers works as a team, and the principle of collective responsibility ensures that the government acts in a unified manner. Hence, the resignation of the entire Council of Ministers is mandatory in case of a successful no-confidence motion. *Thus, this statement is correct.*
 
• **The Lok Sabha is immediately dissolved:** This statement is *incorrect*. The dissolution of the Lok Sabha is not an automatic consequence of a no-confidence motion. Instead, it depends on the President's discretion, who may decide to dissolve the Lok Sabha if no alternative government can be formed.
 
• **Only the targeted minister must resign:** This statement is *incorrect*. As per the principle of collective responsibility, the resignation of an individual minister does not suffice. The entire Council of Ministers must step down.
 
• **The President dismisses only the targeted minister:** This statement is *incorrect*. The President does not have the authority to dismiss only the targeted minister in the case of a no-confidence motion. The resignation of the entire Council of Ministers is mandatory.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is The entire Council of Ministers must resign.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **No-Confidence Motion:**

 
 
• A **No-Confidence Motion** is a parliamentary procedure through which the Lok Sabha members express their lack of trust in the Council of Ministers. If it is passed, the government must resign.
 
• Under **Article 75(3)**, the government can only remain in power as long as it enjoys the confidence of the majority in the Lok Sabha.
 
• **Key Example:** In 1979, the government led by **Morarji Desai** resigned after losing a no-confidence motion in the Lok Sabha.
 
 
 
• **Collective Responsibility in India:**
 
 
• The concept of collective responsibility is a cornerstone of India's parliamentary system. It ensures that the Council of Ministers works as a team and is collectively accountable to the legislature.
 
• If the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion, it signifies that the House no longer supports the government. In such a scenario, the entire Council of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, must resign.
 
 
 
• **Role of the President:**
 
 
• The President of India plays a crucial role in the aftermath of a no-confidence motion. If the government loses its majority, the President may invite the leader of the majority party or coalition to form a new government.
 
• If no alternative government can be formed, the President may dissolve the Lok Sabha and call for fresh elections.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Provisions of Article 75:**

 
 
• **Article 75(3):** The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
 
• **Prime Minister:** The Prime Minister acts as the head of the Council of Ministers and provides leadership to the government.
 
 
 
• **Historical Examples:**
 
 
• **1979:** The Morarji Desai government resigned after losing a no-confidence motion in the Lok Sabha.
 
• **1999:** The Atal Bihari Vajpayee government fell after losing a no-confidence motion by just **1 vote**.

questions.question: What is the name of ISRO's mission launched in January 2024 to study the polarisation of cosmic X-rays?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**XPoSat**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **XPoSat** is an acronym for the **X-ray Polarimeter Satellite**, launched by the **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)** in **January 2024**.
 
• The mission is aimed at studying the **polarisation of cosmic X-rays**. Polarisation refers to the orientation of the electromagnetic waves, and understanding this helps to decipher celestial phenomena.
 
• XPoSat is India’s **first dedicated polarimetry mission**, designed to provide insights into **high-energy astrophysical phenomena** such as black holes, neutron stars, and pulsars. *Hence, XPoSat is the correct answer.*
 
• The satellite is equipped with the **Polarimeter instrument** to measure the degree and angle of polarisation of X-rays from various celestial sources.
 
• It aims to explore the **role of magnetic fields** and their interaction with high-energy particles in the universe. *This makes it a unique mission for space exploration.*
 
• The mission will contribute to the global database for astrophysics and enhance India’s capability in space science.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **About XPoSat:**

 
 
• **XPoSat** will carry two scientific payloads: the primary **Polarimeter** and a secondary payload for monitoring particle flux.
 
• The **Polarimeter** will measure the polarisation of X-rays in a specific energy range to study celestial objects, while the secondary payload will observe the particle environment around Earth.
 
 
 
• **Significance of XPoSat:**
 
 
• It will help investigate **extreme physical environments** such as regions near black holes and neutron stars.
 
• The data collected will enhance our understanding of high-energy processes, magnetic fields, and particle acceleration mechanisms.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Missions:**
 
 
• **Aditya-L1:** Another ISRO mission, launched earlier, studies the Sun's corona, solar radiation, and solar wind.
 
• **RISAT-1:** A radar imaging satellite focused on Earth observation for agricultural and disaster management applications.
 
• **AstroSat:** India’s first multi-wavelength space observatory, launched in 2015, which observes celestial sources in X-ray, UV, and optical wavelengths.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Why Polarisation is Important:**

 
 
• Polarisation measurements can reveal **hidden details about the structure, environment, and emission mechanisms** of celestial objects.
 
• It helps astrophysicists understand the behavior of **light and radiation** in high-energy environments.
 
 
 
• **Future Prospects:**
 
 
• The success of XPoSat could pave the way for more advanced missions focused on polarimetry.
 
• It will strengthen India’s position in **space science** and provide valuable contributions to international collaborations in astrophysics.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of the Control Unit within the Central Processing Unit?

options.text: It displays the processed output to the user.
It performs all mathematical and logical calculations.
It directs and coordinates the activities of all components of the computer.
It stores data and instructions temporarily during processing.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It directs and coordinates the activities of all components of the computer.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Role of the Control Unit (CU):** The **Control Unit** is a critical component of the **Central Processing Unit (CPU)**. It acts as the manager of the CPU, directing and coordinating all activities within the computer system.
 
• The Control Unit functions like a supervisor, ensuring that the various parts of the CPU work in harmony. It interprets instructions and sends control signals to other units of the computer system to execute operations. **Hence, the correct answer is that it directs and coordinates the activities of all components of the computer.**
 
• It does not perform calculations or store data but facilitates their execution by ensuring that instructions and data are processed in the correct sequence. *This eliminates options 2 and 4.*
 
• Additionally, the CU is responsible for fetching instructions from the memory, decoding them, and ensuring their execution through proper communication with the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU), registers, and memory. *This eliminates option 1 as well because displaying processed output is not the CU's role.*
 
• The Control Unit works with other components like the ALU and memory to ensure smooth functioning of the computer system. This makes it the central coordinating unit within the CPU.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Functions of the Control Unit:**

 
 
• The Control Unit is responsible for managing the flow of data between the CPU and other parts of the computer system. It ensures that instructions are fetched, decoded, and executed in the correct order.
 
• It generates **control signals** that coordinate the operations of the CPU, memory, and input/output devices.
 
• It also oversees the timing and control of all operations, ensuring that tasks are completed in the correct sequence.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with other CPU components:**
 
 
• **Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU):** The ALU performs all mathematical and logical operations, such as addition, subtraction, and comparisons. This function is distinct from the CU, which coordinates operations.
 
• **Memory Unit:** This stores data and instructions temporarily during processing. The CU interacts with the memory unit to retrieve instructions and data.
 
 
 
• **Types of Control Units:**
 
 
• **Hardwired Control Unit:** This type of CU uses fixed logic circuits to control and execute instructions. It is faster but less flexible.
 
• **Microprogrammed Control Unit:** This CU uses a set of instructions or microprograms to generate control signals. It is more flexible and easier to modify than a hardwired CU.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Characteristics of the Control Unit:**

 
 
• The Control Unit is often referred to as the **brain of the CPU** because it manages and directs the execution of instructions.
 
• It works in conjunction with the ALU and memory to ensure the accurate processing of instructions and data.
 
• The CU plays a central role in ensuring that the CPU operates efficiently and that all components work together seamlessly.
 
 
 
• **Example of CU Functionality:**
 
 
• When an instruction is fetched from memory, the CU decodes it and sends signals to the ALU or other components to execute it.
 
• For example, in a simple addition operation, the CU will fetch the addition instruction, decode it, and instruct the ALU to perform the addition.

questions.question: If an RTI applicant is aggrieved by the Public Information Officer’s decision (or lack of response), within how many days must the first appeal be filed under Section 19 of the RTI Act?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Section 19 of the Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005** provides the provision for filing the first appeal if an applicant is dissatisfied with the decision of the **Public Information Officer (PIO)** or does not receive a response from the PIO within the stipulated time.
 
• The **RTI Act** mandates that the first appeal must be filed within **30 days** from the date on which the applicant either receives the decision of the PIO or the expiry of the time limit for the response.
 
• This appeal is to be filed before the **First Appellate Authority (FAA)**, who is an officer senior in rank to the PIO. The **FAA is required to address the appeal within 30 days**, which can be extended up to 45 days with valid reasons. *Hence, the correct answer is 30 days.*
 
• If an applicant fails to file the appeal within 30 days due to sufficient cause, the delay can be condoned by the FAA at their discretion.
 
• The purpose of limiting the appeal timeline to 30 days is to ensure timely redressal of grievances and to maintain efficiency in the information disclosure process.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Right to Information Act, 2005:**

 
 
• The **RTI Act** was enacted to promote transparency and accountability in the working of public authorities. It provides every citizen the right to access information held by public authorities, subject to certain exceptions.
 
• Section 6 allows individuals to file an RTI application to obtain information, while Section 7 mandates the PIO to respond within **30 days** (48 hours in the case of life and liberty).
 
 
 
• **Appeal Mechanism in RTI:**
 
 
• If the applicant is dissatisfied with the PIO's response or does not receive a reply within the stipulated time, they can file a **first appeal** with the **First Appellate Authority (FAA)**.
 
• If the applicant is still not satisfied with the decision of the FAA, they can file a **second appeal** with the **Central or State Information Commission** within **90 days** of the FAA's decision.
 
 
 
• **Important Timelines under RTI:**
 
 
• PIO must respond to an RTI application within **30 days** of receipt, or within **48 hours** if the information concerns the life or liberty of a person.
 
• First appeal to FAA must be filed within **30 days** of receiving the PIO's response or the expiry of the response time.
 
• Second appeal to the Information Commission must be filed within **90 days** of the FAA's decision.

• **Key Features of RTI Act:**

 
 
• **Public Authorities:** All government departments, public sector undertakings, and bodies substantially funded by the government are covered under the RTI Act.
 
• **Exemptions:** Certain information is exempted from disclosure under Sections 8 and 9 of the RTI Act, such as information affecting sovereignty, national security, or confidential third-party information.
 
 
 
• **Significance of RTI:**
 
 
• The RTI Act empowers citizens to hold the government accountable, thereby strengthening democracy.
 
• It ensures transparency in governance and reduces corruption by enabling access to information.

questions.question: Which of the following places may receive an amount of rainfall in a single day that is equal to 10 years of rainfall at Jaisalmer?

The correct answer is __**Tura**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Tura**, located in the state of Meghalaya, India, is known for its extremely high rainfall levels. The region is part of the Garo Hills, which experience heavy monsoons due to their geographical location and proximity to the Bay of Bengal.
 
• Jaisalmer, situated in Rajasthan, is an arid region and one of the driest places in India. It receives an average annual rainfall of only around **200mm (8 inches)**, making it a desert area. Therefore, its rainfall for 10 years would be approximately **2000mm**.
 
• Tura, on the other hand, can receive more than **2000mm of rainfall in a single day** during intense monsoon events. This is due to its position in the northeastern region of India, which is one of the wettest areas in the world.
 
• Places like Tura are influenced by the monsoon winds and the orographic effect, where moist air is lifted over mountains, causing heavy precipitation.
 
• Leh, located in Ladakh, is a cold desert and receives very little rainfall annually, averaging around **100mm to 300mm**. Hence, it cannot receive 10 years of Jaisalmer’s rainfall in a single day. *Therefore, this statement is incorrect.*
 
• Asansol, located in West Bengal, experiences a subtropical climate with moderate rainfall, around **1200mm per year**. While it receives significant rainfall, it is not comparable to Tura's heavy downpours. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*
 
• Siliguri, also in West Bengal, is located in the foothills of the Himalayas and receives an annual rainfall of approximately **3000mm**. Although it experiences heavy rainfall, a single day’s rainfall in Siliguri is unlikely to match 10 years of Jaisalmer’s rainfall. *Thus, this statement is incorrect.*
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Tura.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Tura:**

 
 
• Tura is a hill station in the Garo Hills of Meghalaya, known for its lush greenery and heavy monsoons.
 
• The region is located in the northeastern part of India, which is influenced by the southwest monsoon winds.
 
• Areas like Tura and nearby regions such as Cherrapunji and Mawsynram are among the wettest places on Earth. Mawsynram holds the record for the highest annual rainfall in the world, with over **11,000mm** recorded in some years.
 
 
 
• **Jaisalmer:**
 
 
• Jaisalmer is located in the Thar Desert of Rajasthan and is characterized by its arid climate.
 
• The region experiences very low annual rainfall, making it one of the driest places in India. The average annual rainfall in Jaisalmer is **200mm**, and some years see even less precipitation.
 
• Due to the lack of significant rainfall, Jaisalmer faces water scarcity and depends on desert wells and underground water reservoirs.
 
 
 
• **Leh:**
 
 
• Leh, located in the Union Territory of Ladakh, is a cold desert at a high altitude.
 
• The region receives very little precipitation, with annual rainfall ranging between **100mm and 300mm**.
 
• The primary source of water in Leh is melting snow from glaciers and mountains.
 
 
 
• **Asansol:**
 
 
• Asansol is an industrial city in West Bengal and experiences a tropical climate with distinct wet and dry seasons.
 
• The average annual rainfall in Asansol is around **1200mm**, mostly during the monsoon season.
 
 
 
• **Siliguri:**
 
 
• Siliguri is located at the foothills of the Himalayas in West Bengal and acts as a gateway to the northeastern states of India.
 
• It experiences significant rainfall due to its location, with an average annual precipitation of approximately **3000mm**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Orographic Rainfall:**

 
 
• This type of rainfall occurs when moist air is forced to ascend over mountain ranges, causing condensation and heavy rainfall.
 
• Regions like Tura and Cherrapunji experience orographic rainfall due to the presence of the Khasi and Garo Hills, which intercept the monsoon winds from the Bay of Bengal.
 
 
 
• **Southwest Monsoon:**
 
 
• The southwest monsoon is the primary source of rainfall in India, bringing heavy rains to the northeastern states.
 
• This monsoon typically occurs between June and September and contributes to the significant rainfall in regions like Tura.

questions.question: Who obtained the first accurate value of the speed of light using a rotating mirror apparatus in 1862?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Jean Bernard Léon Foucault**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Jean Bernard Léon Foucault** was a French physicist and inventor who is credited with the first accurate measurement of the **speed of light** using a **rotating mirror apparatus** in **1862**.
 
• The experiment involved a beam of light being reflected from a rapidly rotating mirror to a stationary mirror placed at a distance and then back to the rotating mirror. By observing the displacement of the returning beam, Foucault calculated the speed of light with remarkable accuracy.
 
• This method was an improvement over earlier experiments as it provided direct and precise measurements of the speed of light, which was determined to be approximately **298,000 kilometers per second** in his setup.
 
• His work demonstrated that the speed of light in water is slower than in air, providing experimental support for the wave theory of light, which was a significant scientific advancement at the time.
 
• **Foucault's contributions** extended beyond this experiment. He is also known for inventing the **Foucault pendulum**, which demonstrated Earth's rotation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **About Jean Bernard Léon Foucault:**

 
 
• Foucault was born in **France** in **1819** and was one of the most notable experimental physicists of the 19th century.
 
• He is renowned for his work on **light and motion**, including his demonstration of the Earth's rotation through the **Foucault pendulum** in 1851.
 
• His rotating mirror apparatus experiment in **1862** was a milestone in the understanding of the speed of light.
 
 
 
• **Other notable contributors and their work:**
 
 
• **Albert A. Michelson:** Michelson conducted several experiments to measure the speed of light and earned the **Nobel Prize in Physics in 1907**. However, his work came after Foucault's breakthrough.
 
• **Charles Wheatstone:** Wheatstone was primarily known for his contributions to electrical engineering, such as the invention of the **Wheatstone bridge**, and did not focus on measuring the speed of light.
 
• **Marie Alfred Cornu:** Cornu refined the methods to measure the speed of light later in the 19th century, but he built upon the work of Foucault.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Measuring the Speed of Light:**
 
 
• The speed of light is a fundamental constant in physics, central to theories such as **Einstein's theory of relativity**.
 
• Foucault's experiment was pivotal in establishing the wave theory of light and discrediting competing theories like Newton's corpuscular theory.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Foucault's Rotating Mirror Apparatus:**

 
 
• The apparatus was revolutionary as it allowed for direct measurement of the speed of light by analyzing the displacement of a reflected light beam.
 
• Foucault's work laid the groundwork for future studies in optics and the precise determination of the speed of light.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Michelson:**
 
 
• While Michelson's experiments were more accurate, they were based on refinements of Foucault's original methodology.

• **Anatta (Doctrine of No-Self):** The concept of **Anatta** or "no-self" is one of the core teachings of Buddhism. It asserts that there is no permanent, unchanging self or soul in any living being or phenomenon.
 
• **Dhammapada:** This scripture, part of the **Khuddaka Nikaya** of the Pali Canon, explicitly states, “All dhammas are without self” in various verses, affirming the doctrine of Anatta. It is a collection of sayings of the Buddha and is widely regarded as a concise expression of Buddhist teachings.
 
• The verse “Sabbe dhamma anatta” directly translates to "All phenomena are without self." This highlights the impermanent and non-self nature of all things, a fundamental concept in Buddhism. *Hence, Dhammapada is the correct answer.*
 
• **Incorrect Options:** The **Kalpa Sutra**, **Bhagavati Sutra**, and **Uttaradhyayana** are Jain scriptures and do not discuss Anatta, which is a Buddhist doctrine.
 
• The **Kalpa Sutra** primarily deals with the lives of Jain Tirthankaras, while the **Bhagavati Sutra** and **Uttaradhyayana** focus on Jain philosophical teachings. They do not contain references to the Buddhist concept of Anatta. *Hence, these options are incorrect.*

• **Dhammapada:**

 
 
• **Age and Origin:** The Dhammapada is part of the **Khuddaka Nikaya**, one of the five collections of the Pali Canon. It dates back to around the **3rd century BCE**.
 
• **Features:** It contains **423 verses** divided into **26 chapters**, covering various aspects of Buddhist philosophy, ethics, and practices.
 
• **Application:** The Dhammapada is widely used for teaching and understanding the Buddha's teachings, particularly for lay practitioners.
 
 
 
• **Concept of Anatta:**
 
 
• It challenges the belief in a permanent self and encourages the understanding of impermanence (**Anicca**) and suffering (**Dukkha**).
 
• **Example:** The teachings on Anatta are meant to help practitioners detach from ego and develop insight into the true nature of reality.
 
 
 
• **Other Scriptures:**
 
 
• **Kalpa Sutra:** A Jain text focusing on the lives of the Tirthankaras, particularly Mahavira.
 
• **Bhagavati Sutra:** A Jain canonical text containing discourses of Mahavira.
 
• **Uttaradhyayana:** A Jain scripture emphasizing ethical and spiritual teachings.

• **Key Buddhist Concepts:**

 
 
• Buddhism is centered around the **Three Marks of Existence**: **Anicca** (impermanence), **Dukkha** (suffering), and **Anatta** (no-self).
 
• **Anatta's Importance:** It is vital for understanding the nature of reality and achieving enlightenment in Buddhist practice.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Jain Philosophy:**
 
 
• While Jainism emphasizes the concept of a soul (**Atman**) and its liberation, Buddhism denies the existence of a permanent self, making Anatta a distinct concept.
 
• **Scriptural Differences:** Jain texts like **Kalpa Sutra** and **Bhagavati Sutra** focus on spiritual purification and ethical conduct, differing significantly from Buddhist scriptures.

questions.question: How does deforestation lead to desertification?

options.text: It increases humus in the soil.
It removes the top fertile soil layer, exposing hard, rocky layers.
It increases rainfall in dry regions.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It removes the top fertile soil layer, exposing hard, rocky layers.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Deforestation and topsoil removal:** When trees and vegetation are cut down, the roots that hold the soil together are lost. This leads to the removal of the top fertile soil layer by wind and water, exposing the hard, less fertile, and rocky layers underneath. This process significantly reduces the soil's capacity to retain water and nutrients, making the land barren and dry. As a result, the area becomes prone to **desertification**. *Hence, this statement is correct.*
 
• **Impact on soil fertility:** The exposed rocky layers are not suitable for agriculture as they lack organic matter and essential nutrients required for plant growth. This further accelerates the process of desertification.
 
• **Incorrect statements:**
 
 
• Option 1: "It increases humus in the soil" is incorrect. Deforestation actually reduces the amount of organic matter (humus) in the soil because the decaying leaves, plants, and roots that contribute to humus are no longer present.
 
• Option 3: "It increases rainfall in dry regions" is incorrect. Deforestation reduces transpiration and disrupts the water cycle, which can lead to a decrease in rainfall instead of an increase.
 
• Option 4: "It reduces soil erosion" is incorrect. Deforestation increases soil erosion as the absence of vegetation allows wind and water to carry away the topsoil more easily.
 
 
 
• **Role in desertification:** Desertification is the process by which fertile land becomes desert-like due to factors such as deforestation, overgrazing, and climate change. The removal of the topsoil due to deforestation is one of the key contributors to this process.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Deforestation:**

 
 
• Deforestation refers to the large-scale removal of trees and vegetation from a forested area. It is caused by activities such as agriculture, logging, and urbanization.
 
• Deforestation disrupts the balance of ecosystems and contributes to a variety of environmental problems, including climate change, loss of biodiversity, and desertification.
 
 
 
• **Desertification:**
 
 
• Desertification is the degradation of land in arid, semi-arid, and dry sub-humid areas due to various factors, including deforestation, overgrazing, and unsustainable agricultural practices.
 
• It affects approximately **1.9 billion hectares of land globally**, according to **UNCCD (United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification)**.
 
• Regions such as the Sahel in Africa and parts of Asia, including India, are highly prone to desertification.
 
 
 
• **Soil erosion:**
 
 
• Soil erosion refers to the removal of the topsoil layer due to natural forces like wind and water or human activities like deforestation and overgrazing.
 
• This process reduces soil fertility, impacts agricultural productivity, and contributes to desertification.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Effects of deforestation:**

 
 
• Loss of biodiversity: Forests are home to numerous plant and animal species, and their destruction leads to the extinction of many species.
 
• Disruption of the water cycle: Deforestation reduces transpiration, leading to reduced rainfall and changes in regional climates.
 
• Increase in greenhouse gas emissions: Forests act as carbon sinks, and their removal increases atmospheric carbon dioxide levels, contributing to global warming.
 
 
 
• **Preventive measures:**
 
 
• Afforestation and reforestation: Planting more trees to replace the lost forest cover.
 
• Sustainable land management: Adopting practices like agroforestry and crop rotation to prevent soil degradation.
 
• Conservation policies: Enforcing laws and policies to protect forests and prevent illegal logging.

questions.question: What does the term 'halocline' refer to in oceanography?

options.text: A layer with a rapid change in pressure
A layer with a rapid change in salinity
A zone with the highest oxygen concentration
A layer with a rapid change in temperature

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**A layer with a rapid change in salinity**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Halocline** refers to a distinct layer in a body of water, particularly oceans, where the **salinity changes rapidly** with depth.
 
• This layer is typically found in regions where there is minimal mixing of water layers, such as areas where freshwater meets seawater or where stratification occurs due to differences in density.
 
• The halocline plays a critical role in oceanography as it affects the **density and circulation of water**, which in turn influences marine ecosystems, nutrient distribution, and global climate patterns.
 
• It is a part of the broader concept of a **pycnocline**, which is the layer where the density gradient changes sharply, often influenced by both salinity (halocline) and temperature (thermocline).
 
• Haloclines are significant in estuarine environments, where the mixing of fresh and saltwater leads to the formation of a **distinct salinity gradient**.
 
• The presence of a halocline can also impact the behavior of sound and light in water, influencing underwater navigation and research activities.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is A layer with a rapid change in salinity.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Other types of clines in oceanography:**

 
 
• **Thermocline:** A layer in the ocean where the temperature decreases rapidly with depth. It is commonly found in the upper layers of the ocean and can vary seasonally and geographically.
 
• **Pycnocline:** A layer where the density of water changes sharply with depth. This is often influenced by both salinity and temperature changes.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Halocline:**
 
 
• Haloclines act as barriers to mixing between different water layers, preserving distinct water masses with unique chemical and biological properties.
 
• They influence the distribution of marine life by creating distinct habitats. For example, certain species thrive in low-salinity environments above the halocline, while others prefer the high-salinity waters below.
 
• Haloclines also affect the **vertical movement of nutrients** and dissolved gases, which are critical for marine ecosystems.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Haloclines:**
 
 
• In estuaries, haloclines often form where freshwater from rivers meets the saline water of the ocean, such as in the Chesapeake Bay in the **United States**.
 
• In polar regions, melting ice can create a halocline by introducing large amounts of freshwater into the ocean.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Characteristics of Haloclines:**

 
 
• Haloclines are more prominent in regions with minimal water movement, as mixing tends to disrupt the salinity gradient.
 
• They are typically found at depths of **100 to 500 meters** in the open ocean but can vary depending on environmental factors.
 
 
 
• **Relation to Climate Change:**
 
 
• Climate change impacts haloclines by altering sea temperatures and ice melt patterns, which can disrupt the salinity balance in the oceans.
 
• For example, the melting of Arctic ice due to global warming has led to the formation of stronger haloclines in the Arctic Ocean, which can affect global ocean circulation patterns.

questions.question: What does the term ‘satyagraha’ primarily mean in Gandhian philosophy for mass mobilisation and India’s struggle for freedom during colonial rule?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Truth-force**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The term **Satyagraha** was coined by **Mahatma Gandhi**. It originates from the Sanskrit words **“Satya”** (truth) and **“Agraha”** (insistence or holding firmly).
 
• **Satyagraha** translates to **"truth-force”** or **"soul-force"**, emphasizing the power of truth and non-violence as tools for resistance and transformation.
 
• It was a cornerstone of **Gandhi’s philosophy** and strategy during India’s struggle for independence, advocating for peaceful resistance to oppression. *Hence, the correct answer is Truth-force.*
 
• Unlike passive resistance, Satyagraha is not the weapon of the weak but a moral strategy that demands courage, discipline, and the willingness to suffer for the truth.
 
• The philosophy of Satyagraha inspired several movements, including the **Salt March (1930), Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22), and Quit India Movement (1942)**, which mobilized millions of Indians to demand freedom from colonial rule.
 
• The central idea is to **convert the oppressor through love and self-suffering**, rather than defeating them through violence or hatred.
 
• Satyagraha emphasizes the belief that justice and truth will ultimately prevail, and it aligns with the principles of non-violence (**Ahimsa**) and civil disobedience.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Key Characteristics of Satyagraha:**

 
 
• **Non-violence:** Central to Satyagraha is the principle of **Ahimsa**, which means not causing harm to others, either physically or emotionally.
 
• **Adherence to Truth:** Satyagrahis (practitioners of Satyagraha) must abide by the truth at all costs, even if it involves personal suffering.
 
• **Self-suffering:** Instead of inflicting pain on opponents, Satyagrahis willingly accept suffering to demonstrate the moral strength of their cause.
 
 
 
• **Movements Based on Satyagraha:**
 
 
• **Salt March (1930):** A significant example where Gandhi led a 240-mile march to protest the British salt tax, demonstrating non-violent resistance.
 
• **Champaran Satyagraha (1917):** Gandhi’s first major Satyagraha in India, addressing the plight of indigo farmers in Bihar.
 
• **Kheda Satyagraha (1918):** A non-violent protest against oppressive taxation in Gujarat during a famine.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Options:**
 
 
• **Non-cooperation:** Refers to a deliberate refusal to cooperate with oppressive authorities, as seen in the **Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22).** However, it does not encompass the broader moral and spiritual dimensions of Satyagraha.
 
• **Passive resistance:** Involves non-violent opposition but lacks the proactive engagement and moral philosophy of truth inherent in Satyagraha.
 
• **Civil disobedience:** A component of Satyagraha, where individuals refuse to follow unjust laws, as exemplified by the **Dandi March (1930).**
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Global Influence:**

 
 
• The philosophy of Satyagraha inspired global leaders like **Martin Luther King Jr.** during the Civil Rights Movement in the USA and **Nelson Mandela** in South Africa’s struggle against apartheid.
 
• It continues to be a powerful tool for non-violent resistance and social justice worldwide.
 
 
 
• **Legacy in India:**
 
 
• Satyagraha played a pivotal role in mobilizing the masses during India’s freedom struggle and remains a guiding principle in addressing social and political issues in India today.

questions.question: Select the correct statement regarding the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) of India.

options.text: It is a constitutional body formed by a Constitutional Amendment, with powers equal to the Supreme Court.
The NHRC has direct powers to prosecute and punish public officials for human rights abuses.
It was established in 1993 by an Act of Parliament to investigate and recommend on human rights violations.
The Chairperson of the NHRC is the Prime Minister of India.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It was established in 1993 by an Act of Parliament to investigate and recommend on human rights violations.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Statement 1:** "It is a constitutional body formed by a Constitutional Amendment, with powers equal to the Supreme Court."

 
 
• This is **incorrect**. The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) of India is a **statutory body**, not a constitutional body. It was established under the **Protection of Human Rights Act (PHRA), 1993.**
 
• Unlike the Supreme Court, it does not have powers to enforce its decisions. It can only recommend actions to the government regarding human rights violations.
 
 
 
• **Statement 2:** "The NHRC has direct powers to prosecute and punish public officials for human rights abuses."
 
 
• This is **incorrect**. The NHRC does not have judicial powers to prosecute or punish individuals. It can investigate complaints of human rights violations and recommend corrective measures to the government, but it cannot directly enforce its recommendations.
 
• The NHRC relies on the judiciary and government authorities to act upon its findings and recommendations.
 
 
 
• **Statement 3:** "It was established in 1993 by an Act of Parliament to investigate and recommend on human rights violations."
 
 
• This is **correct**. The NHRC was established in **October 1993** under the **Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993**.
 
• Its primary role is to investigate complaints of human rights violations and recommend remedial measures to the government or concerned authorities.
 
• The Commission also reviews laws and policies to ensure they align with human rights standards.
 
 
 
• **Statement 4:** "The Chairperson of the NHRC is the Prime Minister of India."
 
 
• This is **incorrect**. The Chairperson of the NHRC is not the Prime Minister of India.
 
• The Chairperson must be a retired **Chief Justice of India** or a judge of the Supreme Court.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **About the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC):**

 
 
• The NHRC was established on **October 12, 1993**, under the **Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993**.
 
• It is headquartered in **New Delhi**.
 
• The Commission works to protect and promote **human rights**, which are defined as the rights relating to life, liberty, equality, and dignity guaranteed by the **Constitution of India** or international covenants.
 
 
 
• **Composition of the NHRC:**
 
 
• The Commission comprises a **Chairperson** and a number of members. The Chairperson must be a **retired Chief Justice of India**.
 
• Other members include judges of the **Supreme Court** or **High Court**, as well as experts in the field of human rights.
 
 
 
• **Functions of the NHRC:**
 
 
• Investigate complaints of **human rights violations**.
 
• Review the safeguards provided under the **Constitution** and laws for the protection of human rights.
 
• Recommend measures for the effective implementation of human rights policies and laws.
 
• Undertake and promote research and awareness campaigns on **human rights issues**.
 
 
 
• **Limitations of the NHRC:**
 
 
• Its recommendations are not **legally binding** on the government.
 
• It does not have the power to impose **penalties** or prosecute individuals for human rights violations.
 
• Its jurisdiction is limited to public authorities and does not extend to private individuals or organizations.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Legal Provisions under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993:**

 
 
• The Act defines **human rights** as the rights relating to life, liberty, equality, and dignity of the individual as guaranteed by the Constitution or international covenants.
 
• The NHRC has the power to **summon witnesses**, demand evidence, and requisition public records.
 
 
 
• **Examples of NHRC's Interventions:**
 
 
• The Commission has investigated cases of **police brutality**, custodial deaths, and human trafficking.
 
• It has also recommended policy changes to address issues such as **child labor** and **prison conditions**.
 
 
 
• **Global Perspective:**
 
 
• The NHRC is in line with international human rights principles and works closely with organizations like the **United Nations** and other human rights bodies.
 
• It is a member of the **Asia Pacific Forum of National Human Rights Institutions (APF)**.

questions.question: Which tax was introduced in July 2017 to replace multiple indirect taxes in India as part of fiscal reforms?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**GST (Goods and Services Tax)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Goods and Services Tax (GST)** was introduced in **India on 1st July 2017** as a part of **fiscal reforms** aimed at simplifying the indirect tax structure.
 
• It replaced multiple indirect taxes like **Excise Duty, Service Tax, c(Value Added Tax), Sales Tax**, and others, consolidating them into a single tax.
 
• **GST** is a comprehensive, multi-stage, destination-based tax that is levied on every value addition in the supply chain. *Hence, this reform was implemented to streamline the tax system in India.*
 
• **GST is applicable** across the country and is structured in a way to eliminate the cascading effect of taxes. This cascading effect refers to the tax-on-tax situation in the earlier regime.
 
• **The GST Council** was set up to make recommendations on various aspects of GST, including tax rates, exemptions, and threshold limits. *The council ensures smooth implementation of GST.*
 
• The GST structure is divided into **CGST (Central GST), SGST (State GST), and IGST (Integrated GST)** to ensure revenue sharing between the Centre and States.
 
• GST has significantly increased **tax compliance** and reduced the complexity of filing multiple returns for businesses. *Hence, it has simplified the indirect tax system in India.*
 
• It also promotes **‘One Nation, One Tax’** by unifying the tax structure across the country, thereby fostering ease of doing business in India. *Thus, GST is a landmark reform in the Indian taxation system.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Objective of GST:**

 
 
• **GST** aims to create a unified market by eliminating the previous tax barriers between states and simplifying the indirect tax structure.
 
• It ensures that the tax is collected at each stage of value addition, but the burden is borne by the final consumer.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of GST:**
 
 
• **Dual GST Model:** India adopted a dual GST model where both the Centre and the States have the power to levy and collect taxes.
 
• **Input Tax Credit (ITC):** Businesses can claim credit for the taxes paid on purchases, which helps in reducing the overall tax burden and eliminates tax cascading.
 
• **GST Slabs:** GST has four tax slabs – 5%, 12%, 18%, and 28%, with specific goods and services falling under different categories.
 
 
 
• **Implementation Challenges:**
 
 
• The initial phase of GST implementation faced challenges such as technical glitches in the GST Network (GSTN) and a lack of awareness among businesses.
 
• Over time, these issues have been addressed, and the GST compliance process has been streamlined.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Previous Tax System:**

 
 
• Before GST, India followed a complex tax structure with multiple taxes such as **Excise Duty, VAT, Service Tax, Customs Duty**, etc., leading to inefficiencies.
 
• This system led to a cascading effect, where taxes were levied on top of taxes, increasing the final price of goods and services.
 
 
 
• **Benefits of GST:**
 
 
• Promotes **economic growth** by fostering a common national market and removing barriers to interstate trade.
 
• Reduces compliance burden on businesses by introducing a single tax system, replacing multiple indirect taxes.
 
• Helps in **curbing tax evasion** through better transparency and tracking of transactions.

questions.question: The southern stretch of the Western Coast of India, sandwiched between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea, is referred to as the _________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Malabar Coast**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Malabar Coast** refers to the southern stretch of the western coast of India, sandwiched between the **Western Ghats** and the **Arabian Sea**. It is known for its rich biodiversity, lush greenery, and coconut plantations.
 
• The region covers parts of **Kerala** and some coastal areas of **Karnataka**. The Malabar Coast is historically significant due to its role in the spice trade and its connections with traders from the Middle East, Europe, and East Asia.
 
• The geography of the Malabar Coast includes backwaters, lagoons, and estuaries, making it one of the most scenic coastal regions in India. These geographical features are crucial for transportation, tourism, and fishing industries.*Hence, the region is referred to as the Malabar Coast.*
 
• The **Malabar Coast** has a tropical climate, which supports the growth of spices like **pepper, cardamom, and cinnamon**. It has historically been known as the "Spice Coast" due to the abundance of these valuable commodities.
 
• The coastal region has been a hub of cultural exchange, influenced by travelers and traders from various parts of the world, including the Arabs, Chinese, Portuguese, and British.*Hence, the answer Malabar Coast is correct.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Geographical Significance of the Malabar Coast:**

 
 
• The **Malabar Coast** is characterized by its unique geography, including **long sandy beaches, lagoons, estuaries, and backwaters.** The backwaters are interconnected with a network of canals, providing a transportation system and supporting fishing and tourism.
 
• Some famous backwater destinations on the Malabar Coast include **Alleppey** (Alappuzha), **Kumarakom**, and **Kochi.**
 
 
 
• **Historical Importance:**
 
 
• The Malabar Coast was a key region in the ancient and medieval spice trade. Traders from **Arabia, China, Europe, and Africa** frequently visited this region to trade spices.
 
• The arrival of the Portuguese explorer **Vasco da Gama** in **1498** on the Malabar Coast marked the beginning of European colonial interest in India.
 
 
 
• **Culture and Economy:**
 
 
• The Malabar Coast's culture reflects a blend of indigenous traditions and foreign influences. The region is known for its **Kerala-style architecture**, art forms like **Kathakali** and **Mohiniyattam**, and traditional cuisine.
 
• The economy of the Malabar Coast thrives on **agriculture, tourism, and fishing.** Coconut cultivation and spice production are major agricultural activities.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Other Coastal Regions:**

 
 
• **Kathiawar Peninsula:** This is located in Gujarat and is bordered by the Arabian Sea. It is known for Gir National Park and its dry, arid landscape.
 
• **Kannad Plain:** This region lies in Karnataka and is part of the western coastal area of India, adjoining the Western Ghats. It is known for its fertile soil and agricultural activities.
 
• **Konkan Coast:** This coastal stretch extends from Maharashtra to Karnataka. It is famous for its scenic beauty, mango production, and pristine beaches.

• The discovery of white hydrogen in this area adds to the region’s prominence, positioning it as a leader in clean energy innovation within France.

• Hydrogen is widely considered the fuel of the future due to its high energy density and ability to produce energy without emitting greenhouse gases.

• The discovery of white hydrogen reserves in Moselle could play a key role in reducing the nation’s reliance on fossil fuels and supporting renewable energy development.
 
 
 
• **Global Implications:**
 
 
• The Moselle discovery demonstrates the potential for other countries to explore and utilize natural hydrogen reserves as part of their clean energy strategies.
 
• This breakthrough could encourage international collaboration on hydrogen research and technology deployment.
